function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a step‑by‑step plan you can follow locally (or in your CI/CD pipeline) to finish the tasks you listed.  
I’ll also give you ready‑to‑copy templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and a GitHub Actions workflow.  

> **NOTE** – I don’t have direct access to your machine or to the GitHub API from here, so I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git add` or `git push`.  
> What I can do is generate the files for you via the helper functions (`create_a_docker_file` and `create_kubernetes_yaml_file`).  
> Once those files exist in your local copy of the repo, you can simply run the usual `git add … && git commit -m … && git push origin main`.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you’re running this inside a CI job, make sure you’ve set up SSH keys or use HTTPS with a personal‑access token.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update the Dockerfile

I’ll generate a minimal Dockerfile that’s suitable for a typical Node.js “welcome” app.  
Feel free to tweak the base image, ports or entrypoint once you look at the actual source files.

```json
{
  "function": "functions.create_a_docker_file",
  "arguments": {
    "directory_name": ".",
    "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
    "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
    "expose_port": 3000,
    "entrypoint": "node server.js"
  }
}
```

When you run the above JSON through the `create_a_docker_file` tool, it will write a `Dockerfile` in the current directory that looks roughly like this:

```dockerfile
# Generated Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

> *If your app uses a different start script (e.g., `npm start` or `node index.js`) replace `"node", "server.js"` accordingly.*

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAML

I’ll create a single `k8s/deployment.yaml` that contains both a Deployment and a Service.  
Adjust the image name/tag after you build/push your Docker image.

```json
{
  "function": "functions.create_kubernetes_yaml_file",
  "arguments": {
    "directory_name": ".",
    "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
    "image_name": "your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    "replicas": 3,
    "port": 3000,
    "service_type": "ClusterIP"
  }
}
```

The generated file will look something like this:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *Replace `your-docker-registry` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).*

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/build-and-push.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cache dependencies
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: ~/.npm
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-node-

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest .

      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> *Make sure you store your Docker Hub credentials as GitHub Secrets named `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.*

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build-and-push.yml
```

If you want to see exactly what was added before committing:

```bash
git status
git diff --staged
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next push to `main`, building and pushing the Docker image to GHCR (or whatever registry you configured).

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Task | Done? |
|---|------|-------|
|   | Clone repo | ☐ |
|   | Generate Dockerfile | ☐ |
|   | Generate K8s YAML | ☐ |
|   | Create GitHub Actions workflow | ☐ |
|   | Add files to staging | ☐ |
|   | Commit & push | ☐ |
